claims.text: FCC/B2 eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit a transient ductile-brittle-ductile transition with increasing aging temperature.
The initial EHEA microstructure is a lamellar mixture of FCC and B2 phases.
The FCC phase is disordered while the B2 phase is ordered.
The as-cast or solution-treated EHEA has high strength and ductility.
Aging at approximately 400–700 °C induces LCO evolution and phase-boundary restructuring without grain coarsening or impurity segregation.
Intermediate-temperature aging causes ordering, disordering, or LCO clustering in the B2 phase.
LCO-induced lattice strain changes FCC/B2 phase boundaries from coherent to semi-coherent or incoherent.
Strong LCO clusters in B2 increase the Peierls barrier and lattice friction for dislocation glide.
The LCO-induced increase in dislocation resistance produces a large rise in yield strength and a sharp loss of ductility.
LCO evolution changes phase-boundary energy and coherency, creating stress concentrations that can initiate cracks.
At higher aging temperatures, LCO clusters dissolve or B2 disorders, lowering the Peierls barrier and restoring dislocation mobility.
At higher aging temperatures, phase boundaries re-cohere or relax and ductility recovers.
Ductility changes non-monotonically with aging temperature and correlates with LCO and phase-boundary coherency while grain size remains constant.
Impurity-driven grain-boundary embrittlement or grain coarsening would cause monotonic degradation or merely shift the brittle-ductile transition rather than produce transient recovery.
The embrittlement regime is approximately 400–600 °C, where B2 LCO is maximal and phase boundaries are most susceptible to decohesion.
LCO is absent at low temperature and fully dissolved at high temperature.
XRD superlattice-peak intensity can be used as an LCO order parameter.
The hypothesis is falsified if brittleness occurs without increased LCO or changed phase-boundary coherency, or if recovery occurs without LCO dissolution or phase-boundary re-coherency.
A correlation between grain-size change and ductility loss would falsify the proposed non-grain-boundary mechanism.
